awd_titl_txt: Collaborative Research: Supporting Project-Based Learning in Undergraduate Software Engineering Courses
awd_abstract_narration:
This project aims to serve the national interest by increasing the use of evidence-based teaching practices in undergraduate computer science curricula. One such practice is project-based learning, which gives students opportunities to learn as they work on authentic real-world problems. Project-based learning, and other active learning practices, have been shown to increase student motivation and engagement, raise exam performance, and reduce failure rates. A major barrier to implementing project-based learning in the classroom is that instructors must provide students with the support they need to be successful learners as they complete project tasks.  Without that support, students can get bogged down performing unessential tasks instead of learning the targeted concepts and skills. This project aims to increase the use of project-based learning in software engineering courses.  To do so, the project will design, develop, and evaluate a reference software engineering course with a repository of twelve ready-to-use projects and associated active learning activities.  These resources will enable instructors to easily assign project tasks for students to complete at home.  It is anticipated that these resources will increase the capacity of instructors to effectively use project-based learning in their courses.  In addition, project-based learning can help students prepare for industry careers by providing learning experiences that are like the work that software engineers do.

The overarching goal of this project is to increase student learning by encouraging and facilitating authentic computer science learning experiences. Data for formative evaluation of the developed project-based learning resources will be gathered through advisory board reviews, undergraduate beta testing, and in-house classroom trials. Field tests at multiple volunteer sites will assess the feasibility of implementing the project-based learning resources in college or university settings. Finally, a pilot study will be performed to assess the promise of the developed materials to improve student learning outcomes. The NSF IUSE: EHR Program supports research and development projects to improve the effectiveness of STEM education for all students. This project is in the Engaged Student Learning track, through which the IUSE program supports the creation, exploration, and implementation of promising practices and tools.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

Project Outcome Summary

Project-based learning (PjBL) offers computing students authentic opportunities to integrate technical knowledge, problem solving, teamwork, and higher-order thinking. However, despite its potential benefits, PjBL remains difficult to adopt and sustain in computing education. Developing high-quality course projects requires substantial faculty time and expertise, and instructors often struggle to identify projects that are appropriately scoped, aligned with course learning outcomes, feasible within a semester, and adaptable to different instructional contexts. There is also limited guidance on how to organize, support, and assess reusable software course projects at scale. These challenges constrain the broader adoption and sustainability of PjBL in computing education.

This project addressed these challenges by developing and evaluating an adoption-ready portfolio of software course projects and a framework for organizing and supporting their use. The project investigated the characteristics of effective PjBL in computing education and examined barriers to faculty adoption. Findings from this work informed the design and refinement of reusable course projects spanning different topics, scales, and instructional contexts. The project also investigated approaches for assessing student learning, including higher-order thinking and the ability to transfer knowledge learned through a project to new problem contexts. The projects were iteratively developed and tested in authentic classroom settings, providing evidence of their feasibility and applicability across courses and institutions.

The project achieved three major outcomes:

  1. Development of 14 software course projects. The project team designed, developed, and refined a portfolio of 14 software course projects intended for adoption in undergraduate computing courses. The projects provide authentic PjBL experiences and are accompanied by supporting instructional materials. The complete portfolio is publicly available at https://nsf-iuse.github.io/, enabling instructors and researchers to access, adapt, and extend the project resources.

  2. Broad classroom and institutional impact. The course projects were implemented and evaluated in 20 classrooms across 7 universities, reaching approximately 1,500 undergraduate students. The project also supported research experiences for one PhD student and several undergraduate research assistants, who contributed to project development, classroom implementation, data collection, analysis, and dissemination. Testing across diverse courses, instructors, and institutions enabled the team to iteratively improve the projects and examine their feasibility and adaptability in different educational settings.

  3. Dissemination through workshops and scholarly publications. Project resources and research findings were disseminated through two workshops and seven scholarly publications. These activities shared the project's findings, project development approaches, adoption framework, assessment methods, and empirical evidence with the broader computing education community. The publicly available project portfolio further extends the project's reach by providing instructors and researchers with reusable resources beyond the project period.

Together, these outcomes advance the adoption, scalability, and sustainability of PjBL in computing education. The project provides not only evidence about effective project-based learning practices but also a concrete portfolio of reusable software course projects, validated through implementation across multiple classrooms and universities. These resources and findings establish a foundation for continued adoption, research, and further development of PjBL in computing education.
